title: The Office Got Busier. Did Your Cleaning Scope Keep Up?
excerpt: An unchanged cleaning schedule can struggle when more people use the workplace. Review your scope against actual attendance, visitor traffic and shared-space use before assuming the answer is simply more cleaning.
metaTitle: Commercial Cleaning Scope Review: Is Your Office Busier? | YOS
metaDescription: Review your Newcastle or Lake Macquarie office cleaning scope with a practical checklist for attendance, busy areas, frequency and responsibilities.
body:
## When should you review your office cleaning scope?

Review it when attendance, opening hours, visitors, activities or the layout change, or when recurring issues suggest the agreed tasks no longer match workplace use. The right response may be a different task priority, timing or frequency rather than more visits everywhere.

A cleaning scope is the written agreement about areas, tasks, frequencies and responsibilities. If it describes how the office worked two years ago, it may no longer describe the job being done today.

## Count use rather than desks

Headcount alone can hide the pattern. An office with a large team attending on different days may have less consistent demand than a smaller workplace hosting clients and training sessions throughout the week.

Record a representative working week: attendance, busy meeting days, visitor activity and shared facilities use. Include opening hours and access windows. Avoid using a quiet inspection day as the basis for the entire scope.

## Walk the busiest route through the office

Follow a visitor from the entry to reception, a meeting room and the amenities. Then follow a staff member through the kitchen, work area and waste points.

Look for recurring issues and when they appear. A kitchen that needs attention after lunch is a different problem from one that has not been cleaned properly overnight. The first may require daytime responsibilities; the second requires checking delivery against the existing scope.

## Build a simple scope review sheet

| Area | What changed? | What to clarify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entry and reception | More visitors or outdoor material brought inside | Tasks, timing and floor care requirements |
| Kitchen | More meals, shared use or events | Surfaces, bins, consumables and staff responsibilities |
| Amenities | Greater use or longer opening hours | Frequency, replenishment and escalation |
| Meeting rooms | More bookings and client sessions | Table surfaces, waste and between-session resets |
| Work areas | New desks, equipment or storage | Accessible surfaces, exclusions and safe access |

Give each proposed change a named owner and review date. Confirm what is included in the price and what needs a separate quote before changing expectations.

## Separate cleaning from maintenance and specialist work

A routine cleaner should not be expected to resolve leaks, ventilation faults, damaged surfaces or blocked equipment. Identify maintenance issues and direct them to the appropriate person.

Likewise, clarify periodic tasks such as carpet care, internal glass or deeper cleans. Specialist or higher-risk work needs an appropriate scope and provider; it should not be silently added to an ordinary office visit.

## Match frequency to the workplace

Safe Work Australia's facilities guidance identifies use and workplace circumstances as relevant to cleaning arrangements. There is no single frequency that fits every office area.

Review the tasks with your provider and people using the workplace. Agree observable outcomes, practical access and a process for reporting missed work or changed conditions. More frequent visits will not fix an unclear task list.

## Recheck after a move or fitout

A new layout can introduce different surfaces, storage, amenities and cleaning access. Confirm floor and finish care instructions, then distinguish any construction-related clean from ongoing workplace cleaning.

Furniture planning also matters: difficult-to-access areas and unplanned storage can obstruct routine work. Coordinate the cleaning brief with the FitOut and furniture plans before occupation.

## Questions business owners ask

### Does a growing team always need daily cleaning?

Not necessarily. Frequency depends on how areas are used and the tasks required. Review the site and its working pattern rather than relying on headcount alone.

### What should a written cleaning scope include?

Specify the areas, tasks, frequencies, access arrangements, exclusions, consumables responsibilities and reporting process. Include separate arrangements for periodic work where needed.

### How do we tell a scope problem from missed cleaning?

Compare the reported issue with the agreed task and frequency. If an included task is missed, address delivery; if the task or timing no longer fits workplace use, review the scope.
